title: Ham radio operator: varactor cell read non-destructively, then re-read to vote
idea: A radio operator listens for a tone instead of draining a bucket: the storage node is a MOS varactor whose capacitance depends on its stored voltage, read by sending a small RF tone down the bitline and detecting the phase shift; the read leaves the charge intact, so weak cells can be read several times and majority-voted, and no restore is needed.
why: Facts 8 and 1: no destructive-read restore energy or read disturb, and marginal cells are rescued by repeated reads (~3-5 dB SNR gain).

title: BiCMOS bipolar sense amps read half-charge cells
idea: Ideal: a sense amp that sees any charge. Closest: use 1990s BiCMOS processes to build the sense amps from bipolar differential pairs, whose Vbe matching (~1 mV offset versus 10-20 mV for MOS) lets cells that have lost half their charge still read correctly.
why: Facts 1 and 3: ~2x signal margin lets refresh slow ~2x or Cs drop by about half.

title: Eliminate idle refresh: let data decay, repair at wake
idea: When a device enters deep idle, the controller encodes each page with a strong long-codeword BCH/LDPC and stops refresh for seconds to minutes. At wake it decodes every page, correcting the raw BER of ~1e-5 to 1e-4 that accumulated meanwhile.
why: Refresh is 16-33% of idle power (fact 3), and phones and laptops idle most of the time, so DRAM standby power drops ~50-80%.

title: Cast multicrystalline array wafers with grain-boundary-aware row retirement
idea: For the array wafer of a hybrid-bonded array/periphery split, replace argon-purged Czochralski pulling and Spruce Pine quartz crucibles with directional casting under vacuum/N2 in silicon-nitride-coated crucibles, as solar does; photoluminescence-image every wafer's grain boundaries and retire or remap the mats and rows that cross them, since boundaries mostly create leakage-tail cells.
why: Removes two chokepoints (argon, high-purity quartz) and cuts substrate cost several-fold, using reliability mapping to make imperfect silicon acceptable.

title: Factory weak-cell dictionary turns errors into cheap erasures
idea: TRIZ #10 Prior action: each die's weak-cell addresses found at sort are compressed into on-package antifuse/NOR storage and loaded into the decoder at boot, which treats those positions as erasures (one check symbol each instead of two for an unknown error).
why: About 2x correction capability from the same parity, so dies failing today's retention bins pass; a few % yield plus longer refresh at no area cost.

title: Eliminate wordline dielectric coupling: BEOL air-gaps between stacked wordlines
idea: Reuse the established Cu-interconnect air-gap process (a sacrificial polymer decomposed at ~350 C) to replace the dielectric between adjacent BEOL wordlines with air. That cuts line-to-line capacitance ~2-3x, and with it the coupled disturb pulse each activation imposes on neighbors.
why: Reduces capacitive row hammer and row press in tightly packed BEOL arrays (fact 9) and saves ~30% of wordline CV2 energy (fact 10).

title: Deep-trench high-capacitance cells push retention to seconds
idea: No EUV: revive deep-trench capacitors etched into the substrate under DUV-defined, larger cells (~30 fF), so stored charge dwarfs leakage. Retention moves from ~64 ms to ~1 s and the leakage tail stops dictating refresh.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth fall ~15x; DUV density loss is offset by no refresh tax and by stacking more dies.

title: Ferroelectric sanctuary rows hold weak data during idle
idea: Inverts 'volatile data must stay volatile': one mask swaps the capacitor dielectric to HZO in a few rows per bank, forming FeRAM rows on the same sense amps; before self-refresh the controller parks data from mapped weak rows there so the weakest rows need no refresh.
why: Self-refresh rate is set by the 1e-4 rather than the 1e-9 tail (fact 3), ~4x lower idle refresh energy.

title: Magnify threshold only for leaky rows via per-row back-gate bias
idea: Dual-gate oxide TFTs, standard on glass, share a back-gate line per row. Rows with leaky cells get a few hundred mV of negative back-gate bias from a small DAC table set at test and updated in the field, shifting Vt up only where needed.
why: Fact 3: pulls in the leakage tail without slowing every cell, which could stretch refresh 4-10x for tail-limited arrays.

title: Quench-tank immersion screening profiles retention of whole wafers
idea: Like quenching a batch of parts in an oil tank, immerse whole wafers in a temperature-controlled dielectric-fluid bath (no helium backside chucks or He-cooled thermal heads) and run massively parallel retention and hammer profiling at 95C through probe cards, producing a full weak-cell map per die.
why: A cheap, uniform thermal soak lets every die ship with its retention map (enabling refresh-skipping schemes) and takes helium out of test; cuts test capital per bit.

title: Zero ECC storage: recompute-from-lineage repairs transient tensors
idea: Imposed limit: no correction bits for transient data. Only a 32-bit CRC per 4 KB is stored, for detection. On a mismatch the runtime re-executes the producing op from its upstream inputs (the op lineage, as in Spark RDDs) within the same step, so recomputation becomes the correction mechanism.
why: Removes 12.5% ECC storage over 60-80% of an AI job's footprint and lets transient tensors live in cheaper, higher-BER DRAM.

title: Child's tattletale: leaky canary cell decides when each row refreshes
idea: A child asks 'why not let the row tell you when it's tired?': every row gets one deliberately weakened canary cell (narrower access device, ~3x worst-case leakage) on a short split local-wordline stub, rewritten to '1' at each refresh; the in-DRAM refresh engine probes only the canary stub (about 1/1000 of a row-activation's energy) and fully refreshes a row only when its canary has sagged past threshold.
why: Fact 3 refresh tail: most rows hold data for seconds, so refresh energy and bandwidth drop an estimated 3-6x, and the canary tracks temperature and aging automatically; ~0.1% area.

title: Polarity-reversal pulses heal electromigration voids in aluminum power grids
idea: Worse: replace Cu with Ta/Co liners by plain aluminum and let electromigration voids grow until the periphery fails. Flip: lay out the power grid in switchable segments and, in refresh-idle windows, briefly reverse current through each segment so atoms back-migrate and partly close voids before they open.
why: Fact 7 periphery and scarce resources: lets Ta/Co-free Al (or Cu with an Mn barrier) run at higher current density with several-fold longer EM lifetime.

title: Eliminate scrap: sell out-of-spec dies as BER-certified AI memory
idea: Dies that fail retention or refresh specs are not discarded. Each is graded by measured raw BER and retention, then sold as a discounted 'AI-grade' module whose controller applies stronger ECC and shorter refresh. Inference clusters buy the cheaper GB.
why: Turns yield loss (often 5-15% on leading nodes) into sellable supply with no new wafers; a fast capacity lever during the shortage.

title: Diversified-portfolio DIMMs mixing vendors inside each codeword
idea: Portfolio theory cuts risk by holding uncorrelated assets. Build ECC modules in which the chips of each codeword come from 2-3 vendors or process lots. Systematic weaknesses (TRR bypass patterns, temperature-dependent retention) then stay uncorrelated, and chipkill absorbs one vendor's failure mode. Module design, qualification and a pilot run fit in $1M.
why: Makes cheaper second-source dies, including new or U.S. entrants, usable at low risk. That diversifies supply and lowers cost per bit.

title: RAID-5 HBM stack: parity die survives a dead core die
idea: Worse: let one bad core die or TSV column kill an entire 12-high HBM stack. Flip: build stacks with N+1 core dies where the base die stripes each burst across dies with XOR parity, so any single failed die or bad TSV group is rebuilt on the fly and the stack still ships.
why: Fact 6: stack yield loss of 20-30% compounds with height; die-level erasure coding could recover most failed stacks for ~8% extra silicon, netting 10-20% more good HBM bits per wafer.

title: Spectek-style weak-die salvage into ECC-heavy CXL inference modules
idea: Off-spec DRAM is sold through salvage channels into toys and low-end goods because nothing makes weak dies server-grade. Fix: a startup buys sub-spec dies (retention or hammer fails) and builds CXL modules whose controller runs per-die refresh rates, LDPC across dies and a hot-spare die, sold as KV-cache and inference capacity.
why: Turns ~3-8% of output now sold near scrap into data-center bits at ~40% lower $/GB, adding supply with zero fab capex.

title: MIL-STD-883 screening classes revived as a water-lean JEDEC W-grade
idea: MIL-STD-883 defined screening classes so buyers could trade reliability testing against cost. A JEDEC and CHIPS-backed 'W-grade' DRAM class would specify relaxed raw retention (e.g., 16 ms at 85 C), mandatory on-die SEC with host-visible error telemetry, and a certified water cap of 10% of today's litres per GB, with federal buyers and hyperscalers committing volume to it.
why: Water and U.S. manufacturability: a standard makes dry-clean, recycled-water U.S. fabs sellable at scale (~10x less water per GB) despite weaker cells by moving the reliability burden to the system, where it is cheaper.

title: NAND-style bad-block maps let partially-good DRAM dies ship
idea: Worse: scrap or down-bin any die whose repair fuses run out. Flip: ship DRAM with a host-visible bad-mat table, like NAND bad blocks, and sell a nominal 32 Gb die as 30 Gb usable, with the OS or CXL controller simply never mapping dead mats.
why: Yield at leading nodes and in HBM (fact 6, 20-30% yield loss): recovering dies that fail on only a few mats can add 10-20% more sellable bits per wafer without new fabs.

title: First-boot forming pulse punches through HF-free contact oxide
idea: Reverse a defect into an antifuse: without HF dips, contacts keep ~0.5-1 nm of chemical oxide that creates a resistance tail; at first power-up a controlled forming pulse breaks down that thin oxide only in contacts flagged as slow-writing, turning them ohmic.
why: Contact-resistance tails cause write and restore failures; a one-time electrical fix enables an HF-free front end.

title: Wafer-scale DRAM that routes around dead tiles on-wafer
idea: TRIZ separation by scale: a whole 300 mm wafer is left undiced at a U.S. fab; 1,000+ DRAM tiles join through a stitched on-wafer mesh and at power-on a route table skips dead tiles and reticle-stitch faults, yielding one ~1-2 TB memory slab with no packaging, TSVs or foreign OSAT.
why: Defects become routing problems instead of scrapped dies: nearly all good tiles used, packaging and the HBM TSV tax (fact 6) avoided, fully domestic.

title: Eliminate DC bias drift: bipolar wordline pulses heal oxide-TFT traps
idea: BEOL oxide-semiconductor access transistors deposited at <=350 C suffer PBTI threshold drift that grows their leakage tail. During each refresh cycle, the off-state wordline briefly flips to the opposite polarity of the hold stress, emptying trapped charge every few ms so net DC stress never builds.
why: Removes the main reliability blocker for low-thermal-budget access devices and keeps their aA-level leakage stable for 10 years, so refresh can stay ~100x rarer than in silicon DRAM.

title: Federal procurement buys system-level reliability, not component spec
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way around: U.S. government and CHIPS-funded buyers specify DRAM by delivered system FIT (component plus certified ECC/remap firmware) instead of JEDEC raw cell margins, creating a guaranteed market for U.S.-made sub-spec dies remediated in U.S. modules.
why: Lets domestic fabs ship 5-15% more bits per wafer and underwrites U.S. capacity, aimed at U.S. manufacturability and cost per bit.

title: Cheap silicon 3D tiers vote: one bit, three weak cells
idea: Worse: insist every tier of a 3D DRAM has a full-strength capacitor, which is exactly why 3D is not manufacturable. Flip: build a Si/SiO2/TiN/Al-only 3D stack whose per-tier cells are deliberately small and weak, and tie three vertically aligned cells to one vertical bitline so their charges sum at the sense amp, acting as one robust cell whose random weak members average out.
why: Fact 2: lowers the per-tier cell-quality bar so 3D becomes manufacturable; tiers are cheap once stacked, trading 3x cell count for yield, with no W, Hf or Ru.

title: Abolish consumer non-ECC segmentation; create a cheaper raw-BER-graded die bin
idea: Decades of withholding ECC from consumer platforms forced every DIMM to be near-zero-defect, so dies with a handful of weak cells are scrapped or dumped. Fix via U.S. federal procurement rules plus a JEDEC grade: ECC mandatory on all new platforms, and a formal 'raw BER <=1e-6' die bin sold at a discount into ECC-only channels.
why: Recovers an estimated 5-10% of dies/rows lost at test as sellable bits without a new fab; raises supply and cuts cost per usable bit.

title: Magnify bit-significance split: unrefreshed, under-volted mantissa-LSB chips
idea: Bit-transpose bf16/fp8 tensors so low-order mantissa bits land on dedicated chips or banks that run with 4x longer refresh and lower VARY. Sign and exponent bits keep full ECC and nominal refresh.
why: Facts 3 and 10: about half of model-weight bits tolerate 1e-4 BER, so refresh and array energy on those chips drop ~50-75% for <0.1% accuracy loss.

title: Eliminate fixed one-cell-per-bit: dynamic twin-cell mode for weak rows
idea: A row found weak is paired with a sacrificed row in another subarray, and the two are written as complementary twins. The sense amp compares the two cells differentially with no VDD/2 reference, doubling signal. A mode bit sets the pairing, so only the weak ~1-3% of rows lose capacity.
why: Rescues dies that would fail retention or Cs specs (fact 1), adding several % yield and allowing ~30% lower Cs targets.

title: Two-stage synaptic consolidation in NAND-fab charge-trap strings
idea: Synapses hold new memories in fast, fragile early-LTP and consolidate stable ones into protein-synthesis late-LTP; build DRAM-class memory on 3D-NAND-style vertical strings with ultrathin tunnel oxide (us writes, seconds retention, refreshed), and in the background 'consolidate' cold pages with a stronger pulse into deep traps that hold for hours, switching their refresh off.
why: Cost per GB: NAND-style fabs make bits at ~$0.03-0.08/GB vs ~$5-10/GB DRAM (~100x); consolidation tames refresh and wear by applying high-stress writes only to cold data.

title: Optane distrust fixed by endurance-as-a-service telemetry warranties
idea: Part of what killed Optane was buyers' fear of wear-out and an opaque, single-vendor reliability story. Fix: sell nonvolatile CXL memory by the write, not the module, with devices streaming per-region wear and corrected-error telemetry, a per-petabyte-written warranty, and pre-emptive module swaps before the uncorrectable rate crosses a contract threshold.
why: De-risks refresh-free nonvolatile tiers for hyperscalers, removing refresh power from the bulk of capacity and moving reliability risk to the party with the data.

title: Shared per-template repair map for repeating imprint defects
idea: Reverse per-die repair into per-template repair: nanoimprint litho with a non-fluorinated release layer (alkylsilane or diamond-like carbon instead of perfluorosilane) repeats template defects at identical coordinates on every die, so each template is inspected once and its defect map is mask-programmed into ROM remap logic on all dies it prints.
why: Makes capital-light, EUV-free imprint patterning viable by turning its worst weakness (repeating defects) into a one-time repair; cuts per-die test and fuse time.

title: Electrical healing: scheduled BTI recovery epochs for aged periphery
idea: Rule: repair by electricity, not replacement. The controller schedules recovery epochs that apply reverse gate bias and modest self-heating to sense-amp and wordline-driver transistors, reversing accumulated BTI threshold shifts that erode sense margin over years.
why: Keeps aged modules within margin for second and third service lives, so fewer are retired for slow parametric drift.

title: Herd-immunity fleet broadcast of row-hammer attack signatures
idea: When any server's memory controller fires a row-hammer mitigation, it extracts a compact 'antigen' (hashed bank/row-delta/ACT-interval fingerprint) and gossips it fleet-wide within seconds; every other controller pre-loads a matching detector before the attacker reaches it, so the fleet gets vaccinated instead of each chip being infected and learning alone.
why: Row hammer (~1k-activation flips): each die can ship lighter in-DRAM mitigation (fewer tracker entries) because novel patterns are learned once and immunized everywhere; target 5-10x less mitigation area and victim-refresh overhead than per-chip worst-case provisioning.

title: Floppy FM/MFM density switching: twin-cell mode during heat waves
idea: Floppy drives read and wrote either single density (FM) or double density (MFM) on the same media. Subarrays carry a mode bit: in normal weather they run one bit per cell, and on the hottest days the OS migrates cold data out and flips selected subarrays into twin-cell complementary mode, doubling signal and roughly tripling retention so error rates hold at higher coolant temperature.
why: Water: most of a facility's annual evaporative water goes to its hottest few hundred hours; trading ~25% capacity during those hours lets dry coolers carry the whole year (>10x less water).

title: Imprinted nanowire crossbar addressed by stochastic decoders
idea: No EUV: imprint or spacer-pattern sub-20 nm nanowire crossbars of gain cells, and address them through a decoder formed by randomly doped wire segments. Scale shift (molecular randomness -> addressing scheme): each array's random address code is discovered at test and mapped by software, so defects and randomness become part of addressing rather than yield loss.
why: Very high density from cheap patterning without EUV overlay accuracy; tolerates ~10-20% defective wires.

title: Actuarial memory: price DRAM capacity by insured error budget
idea: Combine insurance actuarial models with ECC tiering: cloud providers sell memory at certified uncorrectable-error rates (e.g., 1e-17 vs 1e-14 per bit-hour) based on measured fleet data, with an insurance pool paying out on rare failures, so cheap weak-cell capacity is sold wherever the priced risk is acceptable.
why: Creates demand and a price signal for weaker, cheaper dies, enlarging usable supply; turns reliability margin into a priced product rather than a fixed spec.

title: Honeycomb self-ordering: anodized-alumina pores as litho-free capacitor arrays
idea: Bee combs self-organize into hexagons; anodize aluminium films so pores self-order into hexagonal arrays with aspect ratio >100:1 and no lithography, use them as capacitor templates over cheap stacked access tiers, and handle domain boundaries and missing pores with a per-mat grain-boundary map that drops irregular cells from the address space.
why: Capacitor wall (AR ~115 needed) and EUV/etch cost: an electrochemical bath replaces high-AR etch and patterning; with boundary mapping as the yield fix, a key piece of a ~100x cheaper litho-free cell.

title: Junctionless storage transistor removes high-field junction leakage tail
idea: In conventional cells the tail is trap-assisted tunneling/GIDL at the high-field n+/p junction. A uniformly doped junctionless thin-body write transistor in a gain cell has no metallurgical junction, so peak field falls 3-5x, and field-enhanced trap emission, which is exponential in field, drops by orders of magnitude.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): ~10x longer refresh in a capacitorless cell.

title: Felted fountain-coded pages for UV-LED-printed defect-dense arrays
idea: Felt is strong because random fibres overlap; store each 4 KB page as fountain-coded fragments across 18-20 subarrays so any 16 rebuild it, letting arrays patterned by 365 nm UV-LED lithography with self-aligned spacer pitch division (no Hg-Xe lamps or excimers) carry whole dead subarrays without spare mapping.
why: Defect-dense, cheap rare-gas-free litho becomes usable for a capacity tier behind cache, tolerating ~15-20% subarray loss (capital, scarcity).

title: Per-row-pair SOI back-gate pulses block row hammer injection
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: thin-body FD-SOI transistor | sense: standard | integration: monolithic | substrate: SOI with patterned back-gate strips | fab: DUV]. A back-gate strip runs under every row pair; when row N opens, the controller drives the neighbours' strips to about -1.5 V for the open time, raising their Vt and repelling electrons that migrate from the aggressor channel into victim storage nodes.
why: Fact 9: targets the electron-migration mechanism behind ~1k-activation flips; aims for >20x higher hammer threshold without refresh-based mitigation.

title: Grow the junction first, pattern it later with chlorine ALE
idea: Reverse implant-then-pattern: the access-transistor junction is grown as an in-situ-doped, graded phosphorus/arsenic epi stack (no BF2) before patterning, then cut with Cl2/Ar atomic-layer etching, giving a low-field, implant-damage-free junction.
why: GIDL and trap-assisted tunneling dominate the <=13 fA leakage tail; lower peak field and no implant damage could cut the tail ~3x.

title: Double-length 1024-cell bitlines halve the sense-amp count
idea: Po: everyone shares one bitline. Bitlines grow from 512 to 1024 cells, halving the number of sense-amp stripes; the halved Cs/Cb transfer ratio raises sense errors to ~1%, which the code absorbs.
why: Periphery (fact 7): ~10-15% die area recovered.

title: Apollo restart protection: phase-table rollback survives uncorrectable DRAM errors
idea: The Apollo Guidance Computer survived its 1202 alarms because software recorded restart-phase waypoints and resumed from the last one after a hardware restart. Runtimes keep per-task phase points with a small undo log of dirty lines in a strongly protected region; when the controller reports an uncorrectable error, only the affected task rolls back to its last phase and recomputes.
why: Error tolerance for cheaper memory: turns DUEs from node outages into millisecond recomputes, so fleets can accept 10-100x higher raw DUE rates from relaxed refresh, lighter ECC or lower-binned dies; ~10-20% lower cost per usable bit.

title: Palladium-hydride reservoir re-passivates traps during monthly healing sleep
idea: Time/scale jump (atomic bond -> years): a thin PdHx film inside the package releases H2 when the stack is warmed to ~150 C during a scheduled monthly 'healing sleep', re-passivating Si/SiO2 dangling bonds created by hot-carrier and hammer stress. Years of trap-generation aging are undone in hours instead of being covered by guard-banded refresh.
why: Retention tail and row-hammer drift grow with age; resetting interface trap density could hold end-of-life retention at time-zero values, letting fabs ship cells with ~2x less retention margin.

title: Retread tires: consumer dies plus ECC chiplet qualified to AEC-Q100 Grade 1
idea: Retreading puts new tread on a sound carcass: commodity dies that fail 125 C retention are co-packaged with a small logic chiplet (refresh manager, asymmetric ECC, weak-row remap, thermal dose tracking) so the package meets Grade 1 (-40 to 125 C, 10-year mission).
why: Automotive/industrial DRAM is a constrained premium niche; reclassifying commodity output raises usable supply and suits U.S. OSAT packaging.

title: Minify sense certainty into soft bits via latch-time measurement
idea: Add a small time-to-digital counter per sense-amp group that records how many picoseconds the latch took to resolve. Slow resolutions flag marginal cells, and a 2-bit confidence value per bit feeds a soft-decision LDPC decoder.
why: Facts 1 and 10: soft decoding gains ~1.5-2 dB, so cells can hold ~30-40% less signal charge, or VARY can drop to cut CV^2 energy, with no new cell physics.

title: Sense-amp latch time as soft information for LDPC
idea: Reverse decide-then-correct: a time-to-digital counter on each sense-amp group records how long the latch took to resolve; slow resolutions mean small signal and are tagged low-confidence, and a soft-decision decoder (Chase / min-sum LDPC) flips the least-confident bits first.
why: Capacitor charge wall: soft decoding gains ~1.5-2 dB over hard decisions, tolerating ~30% less sense signal (smaller Cs or longer refresh).

title: Time-to-digital bitline sensing yields per-bit confidence for soft ECC
idea: Timescale shift (voltage amplitude -> picosecond timing): measure how many picoseconds the bitline takes to cross the sense threshold with a small TDC per sense-amp group. Slow crossings flag low-signal bits, and that soft information feeds an on-die soft-decision decoder.
why: Soft information roughly doubles correctable raw BER, letting Cs fall from ~5 fF toward ~3 fF or refresh slow ~2x (attacks the capacitor charge wall).

title: Dedup-as-redundancy: duplicate pages become free mirrors for weak rows
idea: Combine page deduplication with mirroring: when the hypervisor finds identical pages it keeps two copies in different banks only if one sits on weak cells, using the twin as a recovery mirror; all other duplicates are merged, so net memory still shrinks.
why: Retention tail (fact 3) and supply: reuses the 10-30% natural duplication in VM/AI fleets as free redundancy, letting weak rows hold data without extra parity.

title: Hubble's corrective optics: MRDIMM buffers build stronger codewords on-module
idea: Hubble was fixed after launch by inserting corrective optics (COSTAR). Do the same in the data buffers of standard MRDIMM/LRDIMM modules: the buffers spread each host access across two ranks and compute a longer chipkill-plus symbol code on-module. Part of the second rank holds the extra parity, and the module is sold at lower capacity. The host still sees standard DDR5 timing and ECC lanes.
why: Modules built from sub-spec or high-BER dies present spec-grade reliability to unchanged hosts, making ~5-10% more dies sellable (facts 3, 7).

title: Phyllotaxis golden-angle interleaving so dirty-fab particle clusters scatter
idea: Plants place leaves at the golden angle so no two shade each other; map the symbols of every codeword onto cell positions along a 2D golden-ratio stride so any clustered defect (particle, scratch, leaker cluster) hits at most one symbol per codeword, letting arrays be built in a far dirtier, cheaper cleanroom with older tools.
why: Capital intensity: cleanroom class and tool cleanliness are major capex/opex; turning clustered defects into scattered singles that a modest code fixes is one lever of a ~100x cost cut on cheap substrates.

title: Sense-amp latch timing as analog victim-row health monitor
idea: Sense-amp regeneration time scales as ln(1/signal), so a time-to-digital converter on a few sense amps per mat measures the row's remaining charge at every activation. Rows whose latch time drifts above a threshold are losing charge to hammer, VRT or tail leakage, and get a targeted refresh.
why: Row hammer and VRT (facts 3, 9): detects disturbance by its effect, so any ACT pattern is caught, with no counters.

title: Unidirectional codes exploit retention's one-way error direction
idea: Po: errors only fall downhill. Leakage only discharges cells (1->0 for true cells, 0->1 for anti cells), so the controller uses asymmetric Z-channel codes (a Berger-style count check plus a t-asymmetric BCH) laid out by cell polarity, correcting retention errors with fewer check bits than symmetric ECC.
why: Retention (fact 3): ~40% fewer check bits for the same retention coverage, or stronger correction that allows longer refresh.

title: Detritivore economy: reclaim rejected and partial-good DRAM dies
idea: Decomposers turn waste into food; buy the 10-25% of DRAM dies and HBM stacks that fail bin (retention, speed, partial array) at near-scrap prices, package them on CXL expanders whose controller maps around dead regions and runs them at 4x refresh and relaxed timing, and sell them as capacity-tier memory.
why: Supply and cost: fab yield loss is a large pool of nearly free bits; marginal cost ~1/100 of good parts, adding a few % of global bit supply with zero new fab capex.

title: SSD over-provisioning: hidden spare rows with a live remap engine
idea: Adapted from SSD flash translation layers that hide 7-28% spare blocks and remap failing ones in the field: each bank reserves ~2% spare rows invisible to the host, and a small CAM in the row-decoder path redirects any row that accumulates ECC corrections to a spare, copying its data in the background during refresh slots.
why: Field reliability and test cost (facts 3, 9): moves repair from a one-time factory fuse step to lifelong adaptive repair, allowing shorter factory retention screens and absorbing aging-induced weak rows; raises effective yield several percent.

title: AlScN piezo patches strain leaky mats to raise access Vt
idea: Effect: piezoelectric actuation plus deformation-potential band shift. AlScN piezo patches deposited over each mat are biased after retention test so that mats with leakage tails get uniaxial stress on their buried-channel access transistors, shifting band edges and Vt by ~20-40 mV and reducing junction band-to-band tunneling. The bias can be retuned in the field as the part ages.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) and yield: worst mats see ~2-3x less tail leakage, so tail-limited mats are used instead of spared out, and their refresh relaxes ~2x with no new cell-array masks.

title: Hot-row SRAM shock absorber caps physical activations
idea: Ideal: no physical row is ever activated more than a few hundred times per window. Closest: each bank holds a 4-8 row SRAM buffer that captures any row activated more than 64 times in a window; later hits are served from SRAM, so the physical row is never re-opened and cannot hammer its neighbors.
why: Fact 9: removes hammering at the source and cuts hit latency; ~1% die area and no TRR refresh overhead.

title: No per-word ECC: ABFT tile checksums guard weight matrices
idea: Imposed limit: no per-word ECC for weights. Each 128x128 weight tile carries one checksum row and one checksum column, verified for free inside the matmul (Huang-Abraham ABFT). A flipped element is located at the intersection of the failing row and column and corrected from the checksums.
why: Protection overhead falls from 12.5% to ~1.6%, and the checking rides on compute already being done. Weight memory can use non-ECC or raw-BER DRAM.

title: Insurance pool: rack-level erasure coding across CXL memory devices
idea: As insurers pool risk, a CXL switch stripes each 4 KB page across 10+2 memory devices with Reed-Solomon parity computed in the switch, so individual devices can drop on-die ECC, chipkill and most spare rows and may even lose whole banks.
why: Removes ~12% ECC plus spare area per device and admits lower-grade dies; 20% pooled parity covers device-level failures across the rack.

title: Refresh-class die grades turn weak dies into discounted parts
idea: Po: sell the weakness. Dies that fail 64 ms retention but pass 32 ms or 16 ms are binned into refresh-class grades written into SPD; controllers read the grade and refresh those ranks faster, and the parts sell at a 20-30% discount for capacity tiers.
why: Usable supply: recovers dies now scrapped or downgraded, +3-8% bit output per wafer from a standards and business change alone.

title: Self-clearing capacitor electrodes isolate dielectric breakdown spots
idea: Scale borrow (metallized-film power capacitor -> nanoscale DRAM pillar): use an ultra-thin top electrode that locally vaporizes or oxidizes around a dielectric breakdown spot, so a defect becomes a detectable open cell instead of a leaking short that disturbs neighbors.
why: Lets fabs push high-k dielectrics thinner and higher-k (toward the k~70 target) despite weak spots, because failures turn into ECC-friendly erasures.

title: Licensed gain-cell PDK plus scrub controller for U.S. logic fabs
idea: U.S. logic foundries have no capacitor module but can build BEOL gain cells. A company licenses them a bundle: gain-cell bitcell PDK, drift-compensation/scrub controller IP and a qualification report, for a per-wafer royalty. That turns underused 28-16 nm capacity into capacitorless memory dies.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: no new DRAM fab, so supply comes from existing tools within ~2 years.

title: Spider's web: printed ladder-mesh lines survive any single break
idea: A spider's web keeps working when a strand breaks: word- and bitlines are printed as two parallel rails cross-linked every few cells (a ladder or mesh), so a coffee-ring gap, satellite-drop void or crack in one rail is bypassed through the rungs, and the second rail also lowers line resistance.
why: Line opens dominate printed-array yield; the ladder makes yield depend on p2 rather than p, taking a Mb array from near zero to above 95% yield at ~15% area.

title: Eliminate controller scrubbing: autonomous oxide-TFT scrub engines above each mat
idea: Build a tiny ECC scrub engine in BEOL oxide/CNT TFT logic (<=350 C) directly above each memory mat. During idle it walks its mat, corrects single-bit errors and rewrites them before they accumulate, with no channel traffic.
why: Local, mat-level scrubbing lets cells with 10x higher raw BER pass while keeping multi-bit error probability low, and removes scrub bandwidth and energy from the bus (fact 5).

title: Close wordline early, keep row buffer latched to cap RowPress
idea: TRIZ #21 Skipping/rushing: wordline-on time is decoupled from row-open time; the wordline drops as soon as restore completes while the isolated sense amps keep serving reads as a row buffer, and writes trigger a brief re-raise.
why: Aggressor-on time (RowPress) is capped near minimum tRAS regardless of open-page policy, cutting press-induced flips ~10-100x while keeping open-page hit performance.

title: Low-distortion codes: weights stored so any bit flip barely matters
idea: Combine source coding with error tolerance: each 8-bit quantized weight is mapped to a 10-bit codeword chosen by a Gray/lattice-style assignment so that any single flip moves the decoded value by at most one quantization step; the code itself, not an ECC decoder, absorbs weak-cell errors with zero decode latency.
why: Weak cells for AI (facts 1, 3): allows raw BER ~1e-4 storage with no ECC engine, enabling relaxed refresh or lower-Cs cells for inference memory at 25% overhead.

title: Electrocaloric heat-pump layer makes 0.3 fF stacked cells refresh-viable
idea: Effect: electrocaloric cooling. A 64-tier monolithic stack of thin-film cells with only ~0.3 fF planar MIM caps (no high-AR pillar) sits on a P(VDF-TrFE-CFE) or PST electrocaloric film; field cycling of the film pumps heat solid-state toward the sink, holding the stack ~20 K below its neighbors, which cuts thermal-generation leakage ~4-6x so 0.3 fF cells still retain ~16 ms.
why: 10x density: 64 tiers at ~0.2x per-tier density is ~13x bits/mm^2. Same cost: the 5-7 EUV layers and AR-75 capacitor etch are traded for repeated deposition, with the electrocaloric film as a cheap package layer.

title: Eliminate digitization: store neural weights as raw analog charge
idea: Write each inference-weight cell to one level on a continuum of charge (one DAC write, no bit slicing) and read it through an ADC straight into the MAC datapath. Decay and noise act as weight noise that the network is trained to tolerate (noise-injection training). The cells are periodically rewritten from a master copy instead of refreshed.
why: ~4-6 effective bits per cell with no ECC; 4-6x weight density on the inference tier, and errors become graceful accuracy loss rather than bit flips.

title: Two-timescale ECC: light inline code plus strong background scrub
idea: Time split (ns access path vs seconds scrub path): reads use only a cheap SEC code, while a scrubber walking memory every few seconds checks and repairs it against a heavy erasure parity computed over 1 MB regions. The strong code never slows the critical path.
why: Tolerates ~100x higher accumulating retention error rates at ~4% total overhead, enabling longer refresh intervals.

title: Lifetime-matched retention: data expires before the cell forgets
idea: Flip refresh to follow the data's lifespan instead of the cell's: AI activations, KV-cache blocks and network buffers declare a time-to-live at allocation and land in a refresh-free region whose cells only guarantee ~5 ms retention; the controller refreshes only lines whose TTL outlives that window.
why: Refresh (16-33% idle power, 10-20% bandwidth) eliminated for short-lived data, and that region can use low-AR capacitors with ~3x less charge.

title: Segmented sub-wordline refresh restores only weak-cell segments
idea: TRIZ #1 Segmentation (contradiction: refresh often for the tail vs rarely for the bulk): reuse existing sub-wordline-driver boundaries so each 8 Kb row is 16 independently fired segments; a fuse-loaded 2-bit retention tag per segment lets the refresh engine fire only segments holding sub-256 ms cells at 64 ms while the rest refresh at 1 s.
why: Fact 3 refresh tax: ~85-90% fewer segment restores, ~60% less refresh energy and most of the 10-20% bandwidth loss recovered at 32-64 Gb; marginal dies pass without row sparing.

title: Cluster hot pages together so neighbors refresh themselves
idea: Reverse OS page placement: instead of spreading hot pages, the allocator puts frequently activated pages in physically adjacent rows so every potential victim is itself activated (and restored) about as often as its aggressor, keeping cold data out of the hot zone.
why: Row hammer: victims self-refresh, cutting mitigation refreshes ~5x for typical access patterns at zero hardware cost.

title: Telegraph-noise fingerprinting quarantines variable-retention cells
idea: Effect: random telegraph noise from single-trap capture and emission. A background test mode measures a suspected cell's retention repeatedly at several pause times; a VRT cell shows bimodal pass/fail statistics with characteristic dwell times, while a merely weak cell shows a single threshold. Only bimodal cells are remapped to a small per-bank spare-cell CAM.
why: VRT is why refresh cannot follow measured retention (fact 3): isolating the ~1e-6 VRT population makes profiled multi-rate refresh safe, cutting refresh operations ~70%.

title: HDD write precompensation applied to bitline-coupling-aware cell restore
idea: Hard disks shift write timing according to neighbouring bits to cancel intersymbol interference. The DRAM write driver/sense amp reads the neighbouring bitlines' data already latched in the row buffer and gives an extra restore boost (slightly higher or longer restore) only to cells whose neighbour pattern (e.g. 0-1-0) is worst case for coupling noise at the next sense.
why: Bitline-to-bitline coupling eats roughly 20-30% of sense margin at 4.5-5 fF (fact 1). Getting that margin back lets the capacitor shrink 15-25%, or lets refresh run about 1.5x longer.

title: Kinetic-proofreading sense amp that flags marginal bits as erasures
idea: Hopfield's kinetic proofreading gains accuracy by adding a dissipative delay step; add a second timed sensing stage in which the bitline differential must survive a controlled bleed, marking cells whose signal collapses as 'erasures' rather than guesses, so the ECC decoder (which fixes two erasures for the cost of one error) repairs them.
why: Capacitor charge wall (Cs ~5 fF at AR 60-75:1): roughly doubling effective correction lets designs accept ~30-40% less cell signal, i.e. shorter, cheaper capacitors at equal failure rate.

title: Rank-modulated multi-level cells immune to common-mode leakage drift
idea: Effect: correlated (common-mode) leakage drift. Groups of 8 tiny cells are written with 4 charge levels, two cells each, and information is the permutation of charges (8!/2^4 = 2520 states, ~1.4 bits/cell), not absolute levels; neighbors sharing substrate and temperature leak together, so the ranking survives long after levels drift, and a winner-take-all comparator tree reads it.
why: 10x density: ~1.4 bits/cell tolerating ~5x retention drift, on 0.5 fF cells stacked 8 tiers (~7x), gives ~10x bits/mm^2. Same cost: the comparator tree is shared per bank.

title: Eliminate interface traps: transferred 2D-semiconductor channels with van der Waals gates
idea: Grow MoS2/WSe2 monolayers on a sacrificial wafer, transfer them onto the memory tier at <=300 C, and gate them through hBN or another vdW dielectric with no dangling bonds. That removes the interface-trap population behind random telegraph noise and variable retention time.
why: Attacks VRT and the leakage tail (fact 3); atomically thin channels also give ultra-low off-current, potentially seconds-level retention in BEOL-stacked cells.

title: Wi-Fi link adaptation for memory: per-page adaptive code rate
idea: Combine wireless adaptive modulation-and-coding with ECC: the controller tracks corrected-error counts per page and picks among 3-4 code strengths (SEC-DED, BCH-2, RS-4) the way Wi-Fi picks an MCS, storing the code ID in the page table, so parity concentrates where cells are weak.
why: Variability and retention tail (fact 3): average ECC overhead stays ~6% while weak regions get ~4x correction, letting dies with 10-100x higher raw BER ship.

title: FeFET retention loss cured by capacitance-matched floating-metal MFMIS stacks
idea: 1T FeFET memory stalled because the depolarization field and interface charge trapping erase stored polarization in hours to days at temperature. Fix: insert a floating metal gate and size the ferroelectric area at 1/4-1/10 of the MOS area (MFMIS) so the ferroelectric sees almost no depolarizing field, and replace the SiO2 interlayer with a thin high-k layer to cut trapping.
why: Nonvolatile, zero-refresh 1T cell with no capacitor (fact 1); the retention tail is removed by electrostatic design rather than refresh.

title: Minify refresh to data lifetime with compiler-tagged ephemeral regions
idea: Allocators and AI runtimes tag buffers with their expected lifetime (activations, gradients and temporary KV pages live <50 ms). The DRAM exposes per-region no-refresh mode registers, and the controller refreshes only rows whose last write is older than their retention bin.
why: Fact 3: most HBM bytes in training and inference are rewritten faster than they leak, so refresh energy and bandwidth loss in those regions fall ~60-80%.

title: Bounded-error number encoding makes bit flips harmless
idea: Inverts 'binary place-value storage': KV-cache and activations are stored in a code where any single flipped cell moves the value by at most one quantization step (split-unary or Gray-coded mantissa, exponent stored twice), so errors become tiny noise instead of exponent blowups.
why: Removes ECC need for >50% of AI memory traffic and tolerates ~10x higher raw BER, enabling refresh-starved or weaker cells.

title: Relaxed-grade DRAM SKU recovers spec-failing dies with ECC firmware
idea: Dies that fail retention or VRT spec today are scrapped or sold as low grade. Validate them for 32 ms per-row refresh plus host BCH, then sell them 30-40% cheaper with a qualified controller firmware profile to hyperscalers for KV-cache and cache tiers.
why: Usable supply: +5-10% sellable bits from wafers already in the fab, available immediately.

title: Rack-scale erasure-coded CXL pool accepts dies with dead banks
idea: Scale jump (bank -> rack): stripe pooled CXL memory with a 14+2 erasure code across 16 memory devices on different sleds, with lazy reconstruction of any failed bank. Dies with whole dead banks or high raw BER, now scrapped, are sold into the pool because the failure domain becomes the rack, not the die.
why: Raises sellable die yield by an estimated 5-10 points and lets the parity overhead (~12.5%) replace per-die repair area.

title: Magnify HBM stack by one spare die, disable the worst
idea: Build HBM stacks 9-high to sell 8-high. After bonding and stack test, the base die disables the worst core die or failed TSV group through redundant TSV routing.
why: Fact 6: stack yield losses of 20-30% shrink to a few percent; a 12.5% silicon adder pays for itself when bonding yield is the limiter.

title: Noise-shaped bit-plane placement of AI tensors in weak rows
idea: Audio noise shaping pushes quantization noise into bands nobody hears. Weights and KV-cache are stored bit-plane transposed. Sign, exponent and high mantissa planes go to profiled strong rows with ECC. Low mantissa planes go to weak rows at relaxed refresh (about 1 s) with no ECC, where any flips land as tiny numeric noise. The software allocator and profiler fit within $1M.
why: Refresh on 50-70% of AI memory could drop 10x, the ECC overhead goes away for those planes, and accuracy loss stays below ~0.1% (facts 3 and 5).

title: N: liquid-nitrogen memory sled where refresh nearly disappears
idea: A small team builds a dewar-cooled, CXL-attached 1U memory sled running commodity DDR5 at ~77-120 K, where junction leakage freezes out so retention stretches to seconds and refresh is throttled ~100x; an FPGA controller re-tunes timings.
why: Eliminates the refresh tax and leakage-tail errors (fact 3) using off-the-shelf DRAM; cryocooler power is partly offset by lower wire resistance.

title: Eliminate permanent breakdown: self-clearing nanometal electrodes on MIM capacitors
idea: Borrow the metallized-film power-capacitor trick: sputter a ~3-5 nm top electrode (Al or Zn alloy) at room temperature. The discharge at a dielectric breakdown spot then vaporizes or oxidizes the electrode around it, isolating the defect at a cost of <1% of the cell's area instead of killing the bit.
why: Lets capacitors run thinner high-k films at higher fields (more fF, fact 1) because TDDB events isolate themselves; extra margin for low-temperature films, which carry more defects.

title: TSV-free stacks with coded inductive links replace Bosch-etched TSVs
idea: Reverse copper wiring into magnetic fields: since Bosch deep-silicon etch needs SF6/C4F8, stacked DRAM dies communicate through on-chip coil pairs across thinned silicon, with a lightweight link FEC and retransmission absorbing coupling errors.
why: Attacks the HBM TSV tax (~3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss): no TSV keep-out zones or TSV yield loss, and fully PFAS-free stacking.

title: Serviceable-memory procurement rule with open error-log standard
idea: Rule: policy must force repairability. Federal and large-buyer procurement requires socketed or CAMM-style memory and an open JEDEC-style error-log interface (per-row correction counts, PPR history), so memory can be diagnosed, repaired and moved between devices instead of soldered and scrapped.
why: Expands the reusable memory pool and creates demand for repair telemetry. Reduces e-waste of soldered DRAM.

title: Pilot cells in every row calibrate multilevel gain-cell reads
idea: This borrows pilot tones from wireless. Each 512-cell row carries 8 pilot gain cells written to known levels together with the data, and on read their currents reveal that row's decay, temperature and read-transistor drift. The ADC thresholds are interpolated from the pilots.
why: Density/reliability: 2 bits/cell in capacitorless gain cells despite drift, for 1.5% overhead.

title: Zero added read latency: optimistic CRC read, lazy LDPC correction
idea: Imposed limit: ECC may add zero read latency. Data returns immediately with a 1-cycle CRC check, and the core speculates on it. On a CRC failure the pipeline squashes, and a strong flash-style LDPC decoder (~200 ns) corrects the line from a long codeword spanning 4 lines.
why: Flash-class codes become usable in DRAM, tolerating raw BER ~1e-4 cells (cheaper, denser, lower voltage) with no average latency penalty.

title: Four-level DRAM cells read with soft-decision decoding
idea: Po: one capacitor, two bits. Each cell stores one of four charge levels written by a stepped bitline driver and read by a successive-approximation sense; the ~1% level-confusion errors, Gray-coded so they are single-bit errors, are corrected by soft LDPC.
why: Density and cost per bit (facts 1, 4): ~1.8x bits per cell after code overhead without a lithography shrink.

title: Piano tuner: in-field sense-amp offset auto-zeroing during refresh idle
idea: Like periodic retuning, each sense amp samples its own offset against a shorted dummy bitline pair in spare refresh slots and stores a correction on a small trim capacitor or 3-bit DAC, cancelling both mismatch and aging drift.
why: Fact 1 charge wall: cutting effective SA offset ~20-30 mV lets Cs fall from ~5 fF to ~3.5 fF (or AR from ~70:1 to ~50:1) at the same error rate.

title: SerDes decision-feedback equalization across neighboring bitlines
idea: Adapted from high-speed SerDes receivers, which subtract known inter-symbol interference using already-decided bits: even-column sense amps resolve first, and their decided values drive a small coupling-cancel capacitor onto the adjacent odd bitlines before those resolve, removing the data-dependent bitline-to-bitline coupling that eats margin.
why: Charge wall and pattern-dependent failures (facts 1, 8): bitline coupling consumes ~15-25% of sense margin at tight pitch; cancelling it restores margin worth ~1 fF of storage capacitance and removes worst-case data-pattern errors.

title: Kitchen sponge: oxygen-vacancy scavenger laminate stabilizes hot capacitor leakage
idea: A 0.3-0.5 nm oxygen-reservoir layer (e.g. partially oxidized Ru/RuO2 or SrO) at the top electrode of the ZrO2/Al2O3 stack donates oxygen to refill vacancies that migrate under field at 125 C, halting the barrier lowering that raises dielectric leakage over years.
why: Hot leakage drift blocks qualifying thinner, higher-k dielectrics; stabilization lets k~40+ stacks pass 125 C/10 years, giving more charge per area (Fact 1).

title: Constrained codes that never write the worst coupling pattern
idea: Inverts 'any data pattern must be storable': a 64b/66b-style constrained code forbids the stripe and checkerboard patterns that maximize bitline-to-bitline and cell-to-cell coupling, so the array only ever stores mild patterns.
why: Data-pattern-dependent failures, a large share of the retention and hammer tail, drop ~3-10x for 3% capacity.

title: Li: lithium-ion drift trims threshold of weak access transistors
idea: Embed a LiPON-sealed Li+ pocket in the access-transistor spacer; after wafer-level retention test, a high-field program step drives Li+ away from the channel only on the weakest-leakage transistors, raising their effective Vt ~100 mV, then a low-temperature freeze locks the ions in place.
why: Fixes the <=13 fA leakage tail (fact 3) cell by cell instead of guard-banding the whole array; could move tail-limited refresh from 32 ms toward 128 ms.

title: Triple-redundant Mn-barrier copper TSVs with majority voting
idea: Worse: build HBM TSVs with tantalum barriers and accept that one void kills a channel. Flip: use Cu TSVs with a self-forming MnSixOy barrier from a CuMn seed and route each critical signal through three TSVs with majority voting in the base die, so random defects of the cheaper barrier no longer cost the stack.
why: Fact 6 and scarce resources: removes Ta while raising TSV-related stack yield, for ~2x signal-TSV area on critical lines only.

title: Error concealment: interpolate uncorrectable words from neighbors
idea: Ideal: errors that are invisible. Closest: a 180 nm memory-side controller tags image, audio and tensor regions; when a word there is uncorrectable it substitutes the average of neighboring elements, as video decoders conceal lost macroblocks, instead of raising a machine check.
why: Fact 3: tolerates ~1e-6 raw BER on media and AI tensors, enabling relaxed refresh and weaker cells for those regions.

title: Ink-saver encoding keeps fewest cells in leaky charged state
idea: Like ink-saving fonts that print letters with holes, encode each burst with a low-weight code (e.g., 16b to 18b with per-group inversion) chosen using the die's true-cell/anti-cell map, so as few cells as possible sit in the charged state that leaks; retention failures are nearly all charged-to-discharged.
why: Cuts the population of retention-vulnerable cells by ~30-40%, so the same leakage tail (fact 3) yields fewer failures and refresh can stretch ~1.5x; restore energy drops slightly (fact 10) for ~6-12% capacity cost.

title: Parity mat per bank absorbs particle killers from NF3-free cleans
idea: Flip yield from fab to array: chambers are cleaned with remote H2/O2 or Cl2 plasma instead of NF3, accepting more particle killers, and each bank adds a parity mat equal to the XOR of its 16 data mats in the same activation, so a particle-killed mat is reconstructed on the fly without fuse repair.
why: Removes NF3 while holding yield; tolerates one dead mat per bank for ~6% area.

title: Urban-mining refurbishment line for retired server DIMMs
idea: Urban mining pulls metals out of e-waste; this recovers the bits instead. A semi-automated line tests decommissioned DDR4 from retired fleets, maps weak rows, rewrites SPD, and deploys the modules behind FPGA CXL-DDR4 adapters that hide the weak-row map through page retirement. Test racks, adapters and 3 staff fit within $1M.
why: Millions of retired DIMMs a year become supply at near-zero fab capital (fact 4), and recycling also works around the resource chokepoints.

title: No. 1 ESS audit programs scan for silent DRAM corruption
idea: Bell's No. 1 ESS ran continuous audit programs that walked switching tables, checked structural invariants and repaired corrupted records. Runtimes run a low-priority auditor that checks invariants of live data (pointer ranges, allocator headers, type tags, per-block hashes of model weights) at ~1% CPU and repairs from replicas or recomputes, catching silent corruption that slips past ECC.
why: Bounding silent data corruption lets operators relax refresh and ECC strength on bulk memory (refresh energy -30-50%) while keeping corruption risk at today's level.

title: Starlink lifetime matching: 5-year DRAM with higher stored charge
idea: Starlink satellites deorbit after ~5 years, so their parts need not last 25. AI accelerators also retire in 4-5 years, so specify HBM for a 5-year life and spend the freed dielectric and oxide reliability margin on ~10-15% higher cell storage voltage and wordline overdrive. Each cell then stores more charge with the same capacitor.
why: TDDB and BTI guardbands for a 10-year life cap voltages today. Trading them for 15-25% more stored charge (Q=CV) eases the capacitor charge wall without raising aspect ratio and shrinks the retention tail (facts 1, 10).

title: Significance-aware placement puts AI mantissa bits in tail-prone rows
idea: Effect: trap-assisted-tunneling retention tails are lognormal and concentrated in identifiable rows. The controller profiles row retention and packs low-significance bits (FP8/BF16 mantissa LSBs, KV-cache low bits) into tail-prone rows refreshed 8x less often and without ECC, while sign and exponent bits go to strong rows with ECC.
why: 10x density: a ~10x-dense 3D die where only ~30% of rows meet strict retention is still fully sold, with the rest used as 'approximate bits' for AI tensors that tolerate ~1e-4 BER with <0.1% accuracy loss, raising effective density at the same cost.

title: N+1 hot-spare die inside every DRAM package
idea: Rule: a dead die must be fenced and replaced in situ. Each multi-die package carries one spare die behind in-package switches. When a die fails, its contents are rebuilt from chipkill parity onto the spare and the failed die is disconnected.
why: Package survives the first die failure at ~1/N capacity overhead, and the package and module get far longer field lives.
